john-snow.line: In 1854, cholera killed hundreds in Soho in a matter of days.
john-snow.need: Victorian-era image of cholera in London

john-snow.line: Doctors blamed miasma: a poisonous bad air.
john-snow.need: period illustration of miasma or bad air as disease

john-snow.line: One physician, John Snow, didn't buy it.
He marked every death on a map.
The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street.
London drank Thames water full of sewage.
john-snow.need: period cartoon or image of dirty Thames water

john-snow.line: Decades later, scientists saw the bacteria behind it.
London rebuilt its sewers, and cholera never returned.

apollo-13.line: Three astronauts: Lovell, Swigert and Haise.
Two days out, an oxygen tank exploded.
Mission Control had hours to save them.
Engineers built a square filter for a round hole out of tape and cardboard.
apollo-13.need: the improvised lithium hydroxide canister adapter

apollo-13.line: They swung around the Moon to get home.
On April 17, they splashed down in the Pacific.

crispr.line: Bacteria have been fighting viruses for billions of years.
Bacteria keep mugshots of old viruses in their own DNA.
In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier turned that defense into a tool.
crispr.need: photo of Jennifer Doudna or Emmanuelle Charpentier

crispr.line: The tool is a protein called Cas9: molecular scissors.
Now labs everywhere can edit genes.
crispr.need: scientist working in a genetics lab

crispr.line: It's already curing sickle cell disease.
And in 2018, a scientist edited human babies.
